title: Numbers Made of Fours and Sevens

concept.title: Grow a number one digit at a time and stop when it is too big
body: A number made only of the digits 4 and 7 can be built from a shorter one by **appending** a digit: from `x` you get `x * 10 + 4` and `x * 10 + 7`. That is a tree of numbers: 4 and 7 at the top, then 44, 47, 74, 77, then eight numbers with three digits, and so on.

To count the ones that are at most `limit`, walk this tree with a recursive function. As soon as a number is **bigger than the limit**, none of its children can be small enough either (appending a digit only makes it bigger), so the whole branch is cut off.

Cutting a branch that cannot lead to an answer is the idea of **pruning**, the most important tool of backtracking. Here the tree has about half a million numbers at most (2 + 4 + ... + 2^18), so every number is visited once.

statement: A positive integer is *lucky* if all its decimal digits are 4 or 7 (for example 4, 47, 7744). Count the lucky numbers that are not greater than `n`.
outputFormat: Print the number of lucky numbers up to `n`.
hints: Build the numbers by appending a 4 or a 7 to a shorter lucky number.
If a number is already greater than n, appending more digits cannot help: return 0.
Start the recursion from 4 and from 7 and add the two results.

explanation: Every lucky number is reached once by appending digits to 4 or 7. A number above the limit returns 0 and its branch is not explored further. A lucky number of at most 18 digits is below 7.8 * 10^17, so the numbers never overflow 64 bits.
solution.complexity: Time O(number of lucky numbers up to n), at most about 5 * 10^5.
